content_html:
Present value answers a simple question: how much is money you will receive later worth right now? Because money on hand today can be invested, a payment that arrives in the future is worth less than the same amount today. This calculator discounts a future lump sum, a stream of regular payments, or both, back to a single figure in today's dollars.

When present value is useful

  • Comparing a lump-sum payout today with a larger amount, or a series of payments, later.
  • Deciding what to pay now for an asset that will produce income, such as a rental or a structured settlement.
  • Working out how much to set aside today to have a target amount by a future date.

How to use this calculator

  1. Lump sum received at the end: any single amount due when the period finishes. Leave it at 0 to value payments only.
  2. Payment each period and frequency: a regular amount you will receive, such as monthly rent or a yearly annuity payment.
  3. Discount rate: the yearly return you could reasonably earn on money of similar risk. A higher rate makes future money worth less today.
  4. Years until received: how far in the future the money arrives.
  5. More options: whether payments arrive at the start or end of each period, and how often the discount rate compounds.

The present value formula

For a single amount, divide by the growth it would have earned:

PV = FV ÷ (1 + i)n

For a series of equal payments, add up each payment discounted for its own waiting time, which simplifies to:

PV = PMT × [1 − (1 + i)−n] ÷ i

Here i is the discount rate per payment period and n the number of periods. If payments arrive at the start of each period, the result is multiplied by (1 + i) because every payment comes one period sooner.

Worked example

You are promised $10,000 in 10 years and could earn 5% a year elsewhere. Its present value is $10,000 ÷ 1.0510 = $6,139.13. In other words, $6,139.13 invested today at 5% would grow to the same $10,000.

A stream of $1,000 a year for 10 years at the same 5% is worth $7,721.73 today if each payment comes at the end of the year, or $8,107.82 if each comes at the start.

How rate and time change the answer

Present value of $10,000 received in the future, discounted yearly:

Discount rateIn 10 yearsIn 20 years
3%$7,440.94$5,536.76
5%$6,139.13$3,768.89
7%$5,083.49$2,584.19

The longer the wait and the higher the rate, the less the future money is worth today. That is why the choice of discount rate deserves as much thought as the amounts themselves.

faq.question: What discount rate should I use?
faq.answer: Use the return you could expect from another use of the money with similar risk. For a guaranteed payment that might be a savings or Treasury rate; for an uncertain one, a higher rate is common. Trying a few rates shows how sensitive the answer is.

faq.question: Is present value the same as net present value?
faq.answer: Not quite. Present value is the worth today of money you will receive. Net present value subtracts what you pay up front, so it tells you whether an investment beats your required return. An IRR calculator can show both for uneven cash flows.

faq.question: Why is a lump sum today worth more than the same amount later?
faq.answer: Money you have now can be invested and earn a return, and it is not exposed to the risk that a future payment is delayed or not made. Inflation also tends to reduce what a fixed future amount can buy.

faq.question: Can I value payments that rise each year?
faq.answer: This calculator values equal payments. For payments that change, enter each one as a separate cash flow in an IRR or NPV calculator, or value each year's amount here as its own lump sum and add the results.

faq.question: Does the table show what I would have in the bank?
faq.answer: No. Each row shows how much money received in that year is worth in today's dollars, and the running total adds those values up. The final running total equals the present value.
